analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import a 90-day personal supply of prescription drugs from certified foreign pharmacies.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Americans import lower-priced prescription drugs from certified foreign pharmacies was introduced in July 2015 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate committee it was referred to, never receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules letting individuals buy prescription drugs from approved pharmacies in countries like Canada — the same active ingredients and doses as US-approved drugs, up to a 90-day supply, with a valid US prescription. HHS would certify foreign pharmacies that meet safety and quality standards and publish a public list of them. Biologics, refrigerated drugs, and controlled substances were excluded. The bill was referred to the Senate HELP committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who take prescription drugs long-term, especially expensive brand-name drugs that cost far more in the US than in Canada, Europe, Japan, Australia, and other approved countries. They could shop from a certified list of foreign pharmacies and buy up to a 90-day supply with a valid prescription. Consumers who currently skip doses or cut pills because of US prices would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: It directs HHS to write regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to import a 90-day personal supply of a prescription drug bought from an approved foreign pharmacy, filled with a valid US prescription, and matching an FDA-approved drug in active ingredient, dose, and form.

It creates a certification process for foreign pharmacies — minimum five years in operation, quality-assurance and testing requirements, grievance procedures — and requires FDA to publish a public list of approved pharmacies, so buyers have a vetted channel rather than the gray market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who rely on higher US prices to fund their global revenue, and US pharmacies that would face competition from certified foreign sellers. Insurers and government programs would also see lower drug spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes biologic drugs, refrigerated drugs, infused and injected drugs, and controlled substances — categories that include many of the newest and most expensive medicines — so patients needing those drugs would get no price relief.

Even certified foreign pharmacies are not subject to the full US supply-chain security system, and critics of importation have long argued that safety testing and certification can be circumvented by counterfeit sellers, a risk the bill tries to manage but cannot eliminate.
The bill requires HHS to write the rules within 180 days and leaves key safety criteria to the Secretary's discretion, which could result in narrow or slow implementation even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Americans who buy expensive brand-name drugs, the benefit is straightforward: access to foreign pharmacies selling the same medicine at lower prices, with a certified-pharmacy process intended to keep out counterfeiters. The main costs are safety-adjacent risks (imported pills are not subject to the full US supply chain even with testing, and refrigerated or biologic drugs are excluded) and possible upward pressure on US prices if foreign governments resist export. The exclusions cover many of the newest and most expensive drugs, narrowing the benefit. No committee ever weighed these tradeoffs publicly.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors, it was sent to the health committee and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearings, no vote, ever.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 16, 2015 and, the same day, read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
It attracted no cosponsors in the Senate.
The action history ends there: no hearings, no committee markup, no floor vote, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers and US pharmacies kept the higher American prices on their drugs, since cheaper foreign competition was never allowed to start.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and US pharmacies

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and alone carried it; no other senator cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed importation legislation and lobbied against it, arguing it would expose Americans to unsafe or counterfeit drugs.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split on the merits appears in the record.

industries.note: Personal importation lets Americans buy the same FDA-equivalent drugs from Canadian, European, and other approved pharmacies at foreign-controlled prices, cutting into the higher prices US patients pay. This is the industry whose pricing the bill targets.
A legal personal-importation channel creates direct competition for domestic pharmacies, especially on brand-name drugs where US prices are highest.

industries.industry: Foreign and internet pharmacies in approved countries
industries.note: Certified foreign pharmacies gain a lawful US customer base, but only those meeting five-year operating histories, quality-assurance testing, and other certification criteria set by HHS.
